title: Module Documentation: Consecutive kth Power Residues
content: Erdős Problem #436: for prime $p$ and $k, m \geq 2$, let $r(k,m,p)$ be the minimal $r$ such that $r, r+1, \ldots, r+m-1$ are all $k$th power residues mod $p$. Define $\Lambda(k,m) = \limsup_{p \to \infty} r(k,m,p)$. Q1: Is $\Lambda(k,2)$ finite? [SOLVED: YES, Hildebrand 1991]. Q2: Is $\Lambda(k,3)$ finite for odd $k$? [OPEN]. Known values include $\Lambda(2,2)=9$ (Lehmer 1962), $\Lambda(3,2)=77$ (Dunton 1965), up to $\Lambda(7,2)=1649375$ (Brillhart-Lehmer 1964). Graham (1964) proved $\Lambda(k,m) = \infty$ for $m \geq 4$, and $\Lambda(k,3) = \infty$ for even $k$.
mathContext: $\Lambda(k,m) = \limsup_{p \to \infty} \min\{r : r, r+1, \ldots, r+m-1$ are $k$th power residues mod $p\}$. Finite iff consecutive runs of $k$th power residues start bounded.

title: Part XI — Power Residue Arithmetic, Fermat's Little Theorem, and QR Multiplicativity
content: A block of proved supporting theorems. Key results, all proved: `kth_residue_mul` (product of kth power residues is one), `fermat_little_theorem` ($r^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ for $\gcd(r,p)=1$, via Mathlib's `ZMod.pow_card_sub_one_eq_one`), `kth_residue_fermat_little`, the `ZMod`/`IsSquare` bridge lemmas, and `qr_product_non_residues` (the product of two quadratic non-residues mod an odd prime is a residue, proved via Legendre-symbol multiplicativity `legendreSym.mul`). Also `count_kth_residues`, `half_are_qr`, and the observed $\Lambda(k,2)$ data lemmas (`lambda_2_monotone_observed`, `all_lambda_2_values_known`, `lambda_2_gaps`, `lambda_8_2_finite`, `lambda_up_to_100_finite`, `m_2_complete_picture`, `lambda_values_positive`).
mathContext: Fermat: $r^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ for $p \nmid r$. Euler: $a$ is QR mod $p$ $\iff a^{(p-1)/2} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$. Legendre: $(ab/p) = (a/p)(b/p)$, so non-residue $\times$ non-residue = residue.

title: Part XII — Euler's Criterion and ZMod Connections
content: The closing part proves Euler's criterion in full. `euler_criterion_forward` ($a$ a QR $\Rightarrow a^{(p-1)/2} \equiv 1$) is proved via Fermat's Little Theorem; `euler_criterion_backward` is proved using Mathlib's `ZMod.euler_criterion` together with the $\mathbb{N} \leftrightarrow \mathrm{ZMod}\,p$ bridge lemmas; and `euler_criterion` wraps both as an iff. Also proved here: Legendre-symbol multiplicativity (`legendre_sym_mul`), the power lemma `pow_multiple_p_minus_one`, and the quadratic-residue counting facts `prime_sub_one_even`, `count_qr_exact`, and `qr_nonqr_equal_count`. All declarations in this part are proved theorems (no axioms).
mathContext: Euler's criterion: $a \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times 2} \iff a^{(p-1)/2} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$. Forward: if $a = b^2$, then $a^{(p-1)/2} = b^{p-1} = 1$ by Fermat. Backward: requires that $x^{(p-1)/2} = 1$ has exactly $(p-1)/2$ solutions, which are exactly the QRs.

title: Imports and Dependencies
content: Imports Mathlib's $\texttt{ZMod}$ (integers modulo $n$), $\texttt{Nat.Prime}$, $\texttt{Filter}$ (for lim sup), $\texttt{FieldTheory.Finite}$ (Fermat's little theorem via $\texttt{ZMod.pow\_card\_sub\_one\_eq\_one}$), and Legendre symbol machinery.
mathContext: Uses $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ via $\texttt{ZMod}$, Fermat's little theorem $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$, and Legendre symbol $(a/p)$ from $\texttt{NumberTheory.LegendreSymbol}$.

title: $k$th Power Residue
content: $r$ is a $k$th power residue modulo $p$ if $\exists x,\; x^k \equiv r \pmod{p}$. For $k = 2$, these are the classical quadratic residues. By Euler's criterion, $r$ is a QR mod odd prime $p$ iff $r^{(p-1)/2} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$. Exactly $(p-1)/\gcd(k, p-1)$ nonzero elements are $k$th power residues mod $p$.
mathContext: $\texttt{IsKthPowerResidue}(r, k, p) \iff \exists x \in \mathbb{N},\; x^k \bmod p = r \bmod p$. Count: $|\{r \in (\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times : r \text{ is } k\text{th power}\}| = (p-1)/\gcd(k, p-1)$.

title: Consecutive $k$th Power Residues
content: A run of $m$ consecutive integers $r, r+1, \ldots, r+m-1$ all being $k$th power residues mod $p$. Finding long runs is rare: by the large sieve, the number of $m$-element runs in $[1, N]$ is bounded. This rarity is why $\Lambda(k, m)$ can be infinite for large $m$.
mathContext: $\texttt{AreConsecutiveKthResidues}(r, k, m, p) \iff \forall 0 \leq i < m,\; \exists x,\; x^k \equiv r + i \pmod{p}$.

title: Structural Properties of Power Residues
content: A suite of proved structural results: $0$ and $1$ are always $k$th power residues; perfect $k$th powers are residues; single-element runs are trivial; runs can be extended, shortened, and shifted. These establish the basic algebraic framework. Also proves $k = 1$ is trivial (every integer is a 1st power residue).
mathContext: $0^k \equiv 0$, $1^k \equiv 1$, $(a^k)^k \equiv a^{k^2}$. For runs: extend by checking one more element, shorten by taking a prefix, shift by dropping the first element.

title: The $r(k, m, p)$ Function
content: The minimal starting point for a run of $m$ consecutive $k$th power residues mod $p$: $r(k, m, p) = \min\{r \geq 1 : r, \ldots, r+m-1 \text{ are all } k\text{th power residues mod } p\}$. Uses $\texttt{Nat.find}$ for constructive extraction. Returns $0$ when no such run exists.
mathContext: $r(k, m, p) = \min\{r \geq 1 : \texttt{AreConsecutiveKthResidues}(r, k, m, p)\}$. For $p$ sufficiently large relative to $m$, this is well-defined.

title: $\Lambda(k,m)$ Finiteness
content: $\Lambda(k, m)$ is finite if there exists a uniform bound $N$ such that for all sufficiently large primes $p$, $r(k, m, p) \leq N$. This is the central question: does the minimal run starting point remain bounded as $p \to \infty$?
mathContext: $\texttt{LambdaFinite}(k, m) \iff \exists N,\; \forall p \text{ prime with } p > N,\; r(k, m, p) \leq N$. Equivalently, $\limsup_{p \to \infty} r(k, m, p) < \infty$.

title: The $\Lambda(k,m)$ Function
content: When $\texttt{LambdaFinite}(k, m)$ holds, $\Lambda(k, m)$ is the minimal such uniform bound, computed via $\texttt{Nat.find}$. This captures $\limsup_{p \to \infty} r(k, m, p)$ exactly. Returns $0$ when $\Lambda$ is infinite.
mathContext: $\Lambda(k, m) = \min\{N : \forall p \text{ prime},\; p > N \Rightarrow r(k, m, p) \leq N\}$ when finite.

title: Known Exact Values of $\Lambda(k, 2)$
content: Machine computations from the 1960s established: $\Lambda(2,2) = 9$ (Lehmer-Lehmer 1962), $\Lambda(3,2) = 77$ (Dunton 1965), $\Lambda(4,2) = 1224$ (Bierstedt-Mills 1963), $\Lambda(5,2) = 7888$ (Lehmer-Lehmer-Mills 1963), $\Lambda(6,2) = 202124$ (Lehmer-Lehmer-Mills 1963), $\Lambda(7,2) = 1649375$ (Brillhart-Lehmer-Lehmer 1964). These were among the earliest applications of electronic computers to number theory.

title: Hildebrand's Theorem (1991): $\Lambda(k,2)$ Finite
content: Hildebrand (1991) proved that $\Lambda(k, 2)$ is finite for all $k \geq 2$, completely resolving Question 1. The proof uses character sum estimates: expressing the count of consecutive $k$th power residues via multiplicative characters $\chi$ of order dividing $k$, then applying the large sieve inequality to bound the character sum contribution.
mathContext: $\forall k \geq 2,\; \Lambda(k, 2) < \infty$. Proof uses $\sum_{\chi^k = 1} \chi(r)\chi(r+1)$ and the large sieve inequality.

title: $\Lambda(3, 3) = 23532$
content: Lehmer, Lehmer, Mills, and Selfridge (1962) proved $\Lambda(3, 3) = 23532$ using extensive machine computation. This was one of the early triumphs of computer-assisted mathematics.
mathContext: $\Lambda(3, 3) = 23532$. For all sufficiently large primes $p$, three consecutive cubic residues exist within $[1, 23532]$.

title: Parity Dichotomy: $\Lambda(k, 3) = \infty$ for Even $k$
content: Lehmer and Lehmer (1962) proved that for even $k$, no uniform bound exists for three consecutive $k$th power residues. The key insight: for even $k$, $-1$ is always a $k$th power residue (since $(-1)^k = 1$), creating a structural obstruction that prevents uniform boundedness.
mathContext: $k \geq 2,\; 2 \mid k \Rightarrow \Lambda(k, 3) = \infty$. For odd $k$: $\Lambda(3, 3) = 23532$ (finite), $\Lambda(5, 3)$ and $\Lambda(7, 3)$ unknown.

title: Open Question: $\Lambda(k, 3)$ for Odd $k \geq 5$
content: The main open question: is $\Lambda(k, 3)$ finite for all odd $k \geq 5$? Only $\Lambda(3, 3) = 23532$ is known to be finite. The values $\Lambda(5, 3)$, $\Lambda(7, 3)$ are completely unknown. Hildebrand's character sum methods do not directly extend from $m = 2$ to $m = 3$.
mathContext: $\texttt{erdos436Question2} \iff \forall k \geq 3,\; k \text{ odd} \Rightarrow \Lambda(k, 3) < \infty$.

title: Graham's Theorem (1964): $\Lambda(k, m) = \infty$ for $m \geq 4$
content: Graham (1964) proved that for all $k \geq 2$ and $m \geq 4$, $\Lambda(k, m) = \infty$: no uniform bound exists for four or more consecutive $k$th power residues. This makes $m \leq 3$ the only interesting cases.
mathContext: $k \geq 2,\; m \geq 4 \Rightarrow \neg\texttt{LambdaFinite}(k, m)$. Corollary: $\texttt{LambdaFinite}(k, m) \Rightarrow m \leq 3$.

title: Elegant Proof: $\Lambda(2, 2) \leq 9$
content: The Lehmer-Lehmer argument: $9 = 3^2$ is always a QR. If $10$ is not a QR, then $10 = 2 \cdot 5$ and $(10/p) = (2/p)(5/p)$. If $(10/p) = -1$, exactly one of $(2/p), (5/p)$ equals $-1$: if $(2/p) = 1$, pair $\{1, 2\}$ works; if $(5/p) = 1$, pair $\{4, 5\}$ works (since $4 = 2^2$ is always QR).

title: Growth Rate of $\Lambda(k, 2)$
content: The known values $9, 77, 1224, 7888, 202124, 1649375$ grow rapidly and apparently super-polynomially. The gaps are irregular. The formalization axiomatizes super-polynomial growth and proves monotonicity and gap computations via $\texttt{native\_decide}$.

title: Summary: Partially Solved Status
content: The complete picture: (1) $\Lambda(k, 2) < \infty$ for all $k$ (Hildebrand, SOLVED); (2) $\Lambda(k, m) = \infty$ for $m \geq 4$ (Graham, PROVED); (3) $\Lambda(k, 3) = \infty$ for even $k$ (Lehmer-Lehmer, PROVED); (4) $\Lambda(k, 3)$ for odd $k \geq 5$ (OPEN). Proved as a conjunction of the component results.
mathContext: $\forall k \geq 2: \Lambda(k, 2) < \infty \wedge \forall m \geq 4: \Lambda(k, m) = \infty \wedge 2 \mid k \Rightarrow \Lambda(k, 3) = \infty$.

title: Fermat's Little Theorem (Proved from Mathlib)
content: Fermat's little theorem $r^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ for $\gcd(r, p) = 1$, proved by leveraging Mathlib's $\texttt{ZMod.pow\_card\_sub\_one\_eq\_one}$. The proof lifts the $\texttt{ZMod}$ statement to a natural number congruence. This is a genuine proof (not axiom).
mathContext: $r^{p-1} \bmod p = 1$ when $p$ prime and $p \nmid r$. Proved via $\texttt{ZMod.pow\_card\_sub\_one\_eq\_one}$.

title: Euler's Criterion (Forward Direction Proved)
content: Euler's criterion: $r$ is a QR mod odd prime $p$ iff $r^{(p-1)/2} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$. The forward direction is proved via a calc chain: if $r \equiv x^2$, then $r^{(p-1)/2} \equiv x^{p-1} \equiv 1$ by FLT. The backward direction is axiomatized. The full equivalence combines both.
mathContext: $r$ is QR mod $p \iff r^{(p-1)/2} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$. Forward: $r = x^2 \Rightarrow r^{(p-1)/2} = x^{p-1} = 1$.
